education.title: Education
education.note: The smartphone is both a tool and a distraction: used pedagogically it improves access to knowledge, but recreational use in class is associated with lower performance (OECD/PISA 2022). The key is the design of use, not just the device.

risks.title: Digital risks
risks.note: Figures combine definitions from several sources (EU Kids Online, WHO-HBSC, INHOPE, meta-analyses). Cyberbullying and problematic use are the most prevalent and best-documented risks; grooming and sextortion are less frequent but high-impact.

family.title: Family and parental mediation
family.subtitle: Rules, supervision, parental controls and age of giving the first smartphone.
family.agesTitle: Age of giving the first smartphone
family.note: Evidence favors active mediation (accompanying, talking, agreeing on rules) over pure restriction or covert surveillance: it improves digital literacy and reduces risks without harming trust.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions and methodology
faq.subtitle: How it is built, how to read it and how to cite it. Full transparency.
faq.a1: Not all of it. Each indicator has a status: verified (a citable figure from a specific report/study) or estimate (a plausible synthesis of several sources, order of magnitude). The Library only contains real studies with their DOI/source. Before citing, verify in the original source.
faq.q2: Does smartphone use cause mental health problems?
faq.a2: The evidence shows associations, not direct causation. The average effect between screen time and wellbeing is small-to-moderate (Orben & Przybylski, 2019) and depends on the type of use, context and prior factors. That is why the Observatory repeats the “correlation ≠ causation” seal.
faq.q3: Where does the data come from?
faq.a3: A Python ETL (build_data.py) curates figures from public sources (UNICEF, WHO/HBSC, OECD/PISA, Pew, Common Sense, DataReportal/ITU, INEI/MINSA/MINEDU) and outputs JSON with status and source. A GitHub Action regenerates and publishes them monthly.
faq.q4: How do I cite the Observatory or a study?
faq.a4: For a study, use its DOI and the original source (“DOI →” button in the Library). For the platform, cite the Global Observatory of Smartphone Use among Adolescents (C. Cárdenas) and its URL. Note that estimate figures are syntheses.
faq.a5: Yes. The Researchers module lets you filter and export as CSV or JSON. Raw JSON is at /data/*.json (e.g. /data/countries.json).
faq.q6: Is it available in other languages?
faq.a6: Yes: the platform is presented in the 10 most-used languages (English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, French, Arabic, Bengali, Portuguese, Russian, Indonesian), with RTL support for Arabic. The interface is translated; some long texts and the data content may appear in English/Spanish while review is completed.
faq.q7: How do I contribute or report an error?
faq.a7: The project is open on GitHub. You can open an issue or a PR adding studies/sources to build_data.py with their DOI.

corr.note: Small-to-moderate positive association reported in the literature (not causal). See Twenge 2018, Riehm 2019, Orben & Przybylski 2019.

2005.d: YouTube is born; online video starts to go mainstream.

2007.d: Apple launches the iPhone: the modern smartphone era begins.

2010.d: Instagram popularizes the social photo; the iPad arrives.

2011.d: Snapchat introduces ephemeral content among teens.

2016.d: ByteDance launches Douyin/TikTok; the rise of short video.

2017.d: The smartphone becomes the majority among teens in high-income countries.

2018.d: The scientific debate on screens and well-being intensifies.

2020.d: Lockdowns spike screen use and remote learning.

2022.d: OpenAI launches ChatGPT (Nov 2022): generative AI breaks through.

2023.d: States and countries debate age limits and addictive design.

2024.d: Haidt popularizes the thesis; WHO-HBSC quantifies problematic use.

2025.d: A wave of smartphone bans in schools grows.
